title: Word order: who does what
explain: Chinese sentences follow the same basic order as English: subject, verb, object. 我喝茶 means 'I drink tea'.
Verbs never change. There is no past-tense ending, no plural and no 'he drinks' form. 我喝, 他喝 and 我们喝 all use the same 喝.

Words that say when and where normally come before the verb, not after it. 我昨天在家 means 'I was at home yesterday'. 爸爸晚上在家工作 means 'Dad works at home in the evening'. Time usually comes first, then place. (There are a few exceptions you will meet later, such as 我住在学校 and how long something lasted, 我住了三天.)

examples.en: Dad works at home in the evening.

mistakes: Do not put the place or the time after the verb the way English does. Say 我在家吃饭 (I eat at home), not 我吃饭在家.

q.en: Dad works at home in the evening.
q.explain: Subject, then time, then place, then the verb.

q.en: We are going to school tomorrow.
q.explain: The time word 明天 comes before the verb 去.
The verb goes between the subject and the object.
Place words go before the verb: 在家 comes before 吃饭.

q.prompt: Which sentence says: I study Chinese at school?
q.explain: Where you do it (在学校) comes before the verb.

title: 是: A is B
explain: 是 links two nouns: 他是我的朋友 means 'He is my friend'. 我是学生 means 'I am a student'. It works like 'is / am / are' with nouns.

In a plain statement, do not put 是 before an adjective. Say 她很漂亮, not 她是很漂亮 (see the lesson on describing things). Later you will meet 是 with an adjective for emphasis, but do not use it for plain description.
To say no, put 不 in front: 我不是老师。 To ask a yes/no question, add 吗: 你是学生吗？
mistakes: In a plain statement do not put 是 before an adjective: 今天很冷 is the normal way, 今天是很冷 is not.

q.explain: A + 是 + B.
是 links two nouns.
Adjectives do not take 是.
Say the statement, then add 吗 at the end.
不 goes in front of 是.

title: Describing things: 很, 太, 真, 非常, 有点儿
explain: An adjective can be the whole predicate. There is no 是: 今天很冷 means 'It is cold today'.

Usually 很 goes before the adjective. In a plain statement it often means just 'is' rather than a strong 'very': 她很忙. A bare adjective with nothing in front, like 她忙, sounds like a comparison ('she is busy, but others are not').
For stronger feeling use 非常 (very, extremely), 真 (really) or 太…了 (too, so): 今天太冷了！ 有点儿 means 'a bit' and is often used for something you do not like: 今天有点儿冷.
To say not, put 不 before the adjective and leave out 很: 这个房间不大。

examples.en: I am a bit busy today.

mistakes: For plain description do not use 是 with an adjective: 她很漂亮, not 她是很漂亮.
太…了 can mean 'too' (太贵了, too expensive) or 'so / how' (太好了！ That is great!).

q.explain: 太 goes before the adjective and 了 comes at the end.
很 links the subject and the adjective.

q.prompt: Which sentence says: This room is not big?
q.explain: 不 goes straight before the adjective. No 是.
真 means 'really' and goes before the adjective.

q.en: I am a bit busy today.
q.explain: 有点儿 goes before the adjective.

title: Yes/no questions with 吗
explain: Say a normal statement and add 吗 at the end: 你是学生吗？ The word order does not change.
Answer with the verb: 你喝茶吗？ — 喝。 or 不喝。 For 是 questions, answer 是 or 不是.

A plain verb + 吗 question asks about a fact or a habit. 你喝茶吗？ means 'Do you drink tea?' It is not an offer. To offer something or ask what someone would like, use 想: 你想喝茶吗？ (see the lesson on 想 and 要).

Do not use 吗 in a question that is already asked by a question word: say 你叫什么名字？ (not 你叫什么名字吗？). (A question word hidden inside a bigger sentence can still take 吗: 你知道他在哪里吗？ means 'Do you know where he is?')
mistakes: If 什么, 谁 or 哪儿 is already asking the question, leave 吗 off.
你喝茶吗？ asks whether you drink tea in general. To offer tea, say 你想喝茶吗？

q.explain: Say the statement, then add 吗 at the end.
什么 already asks the question, so 吗 is not needed.
吗 turns a statement into a yes/no question.
Statement order stays the same. 吗 goes last.

q.prompt: Which sentence offers someone tea: 'Would you like some tea?'
q.explain: 你喝茶吗？ only asks whether you drink tea. 想 makes it an offer.

title: Question words: 什么, 谁, 哪儿, 几, 多少, 怎么
explain: The question word goes where the answer would go. 你吃什么？ is answered with 我吃米饭. 她是谁？ is answered with 她是我的老师.

Common ones: 什么 (what), 谁 (who), 哪儿 or 哪里 (where), 哪 + measure word (which: 哪个, 哪本书), 几 (how many, small numbers, with a measure word), 多少 (how many, how much), 怎么 (how: 这个字怎么读), 怎么样 (how about it, how is it), 什么时候 (when).
Do not add 吗 to these questions when the question word is the thing being asked.

examples.en: What do you want to eat?
How many people are in your family?
How do you read this character?

mistakes: Use 几 for small numbers and put a measure word after it (几口人, 几岁). Use 多少 for bigger or unknown amounts, like 多少钱.

q.explain: 哪儿 sits where the answer (a place) would go.
多少 asks about amounts like prices.

q.en: How many people are in your family?
q.explain: 几 is followed by a measure word.
怎么样 asks how something is.

q.en: What do you want to eat?
q.explain: 什么 already asks the question.

title: Saying no: 不, 没(有), 不要
explain: 不 negates most things: 是, adjectives, habits, plans and wanting. 我不是老师。我不喝茶。这个不大。
没(有) negates 有 and things that did not happen: 我没有钱。小明今天没上学。Never say 不有. 'Have' is always negated with 没.
不要 is a command, 'don't!': 不要说话！ It can also be a firm refusal. For a plain 'I don't want to', 不想 is the safe choice: 我不想吃。
Tone change: 不 is said bú before a fourth-tone syllable. 不是 is bú shì, and 不要 is búyào.

examples.en: Xiaoming did not go to school today.

mistakes: Do not say 我不有钱. 'Have' is negated with 没: 我没有钱.
不要 is 'don't!'. For 'I don't want to', say 我不想…

q.explain: 没有 is the negative of 有.
不 negates 是.

q.prompt: Which sentence says: I have no money?
q.explain: 有 is negated with 没, never 不.

q.en: Xiaoming did not go to school today.
q.explain: 没 says it did not happen.

q.prompt: Which sentence says: Don't talk here!
q.explain: 不要 is the command 'don't'. 不想 would mean 'do not want to'.

title: 有: having something
explain: 有 means 'to have': 我有一个哥哥。我有两本书。
The negative is 没有, never 不有: 我没有手机。
Ask with 吗, or with 有没有: 你有手机吗？ or 你有没有手机？
有 is also used for 'there is / there are'. See the lesson on places and positions.
mistakes: Do not add 吗 to 有没有: say 你有没有手机？ or 你有手机吗？, not both.

q.explain: Subject + 有 + amount + thing.
没有 is the negative of 有.
有 means to have.
有没有 already makes the question, so there is no 吗.
Statement + 吗.

title: Pronouns and 们
explain: 我 I, 你 you, 他 he, 她 she, 它 it. Plurals: 我们 we, 你们 you (more than one), 他们 they (people, or a mixed group), 她们 they (all women), 它们 they (things or animals). He, she and it all sound like tā.
您 is a polite 'you' for one person: 老师，您好！ 大家 means 'everyone'.
们 makes plurals for people: 同学们, 孩子们. Do not use 们 after a number: 三个学生, not 三个学生们.
小 in front of a name makes it friendly, like 小明.
mistakes: Do not add 们 after a number: 三个学生 is right.

q.explain: 她们 is 'they' for women.
我们 means 'we'.
您 is the polite 'you'.
After a number, 们 is not used.
大家 already means 'everyone'.

title: 的: belonging and describing
explain: 的 links an owner or a describing phrase to a noun: 我妈妈的手机 means 'my mom's phone'. 好吃的米饭 means 'tasty rice'.
With family and close groups, 的 is usually left out: 我妈妈, 我家, 我们学校. For things, 的 is the normal choice: 我的书, 我的手机. (In casual speech it is sometimes dropped.)
The noun can be dropped when it is clear: 这是我的。 means 'This is mine.'
A short adjective often joins the noun directly: 新手机 (a new phone). With 很 or a longer phrase, add 的: 很好吃的米饭 (very tasty rice).
mistakes: 我的妈妈 is not wrong, but in everyday speech people say 我妈妈.

q.explain: Owner + 的 + thing.
的 links the owner and the thing.
The describing phrase goes before 的 and the noun.

q.prompt: Which sentence says: This is mine?
q.explain: 我的 is 'mine'. 这是我 would mean 'This is me'.
The owner goes before 的.
